title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section distills recent, reputable findings from PubMed/PMC, JAMA Network, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, Nature, and sleep-medicine guidelines; citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This week's theme: the longevity-supplement field is maturing enough to **rank the evidence**, while skin anti-aging keeps validating both the old gold standard and gentler alternatives.

- **Supplements, ranked by evidence.** A 2026 comparative review (*J. Biomedical Science*) put the three most-hyped "longevity" supplements side by side: **urolithin A** now has ~10 human randomized studies (~492 participants) and the most *coherent* profile — mechanism, biomarkers, and early function all line up for **mitochondrial health, muscle endurance, and immune aging**. **Spermidine** stays biologically plausible but clinically unproven, and **NAD+ precursors (NR/NMN)** reliably raise NAD+ biomarkers yet show inconsistent functional anti-aging effects. Notably, an **NIH/NIA** urolithin A trial on glucose metabolism in adults 55+ (NCT06274749) **began recruiting today, Nov 19, 2026**.
- **Drugs & senolytics: still investigational.** A 2026 geroprotective-pharmacology review concluded **rapamycin and metformin** have the deepest preclinical data but **no proven healthspan benefit in healthy adults** yet; **taurine** is an "emerging candidate," not validated. A separate 2026 systematic review of **senolytics/senomorphics** (6 completed human studies) found **dasatinib + quercetin** produced preliminary functional and biomarker effects but called the whole class **investigational, not established**.
- **Topicals & procedures.** A 2026 meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 1,361 patients) reaffirmed **topical tretinoin** significantly improves both fine and coarse photodamage wrinkles — still the best-evidenced topical. A new 16-week RCT (n=79) found **almond oil** matched **tretinoin 0.025%** on wrinkle reduction with less irritation (watch a slight pigmentation uptick). For devices/procedures, a sham-controlled RCT of a **home LED/IRED mask** improved crow's-feet, and a split-face RCT of **adipose stem-cell exosomes + microneedling** beat saved-control microneedling on global aesthetic score.

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "reverse aging" claims skeptically.

sections.body:
New 2026 RCTs keep HIIT as a **time-efficient** cardio-metabolic tool for women — with a consistent message to **add resistance training** for the best body-composition results.

- **Postmenopausal women (overweight/obesity).** A 2026 RCT (*Explor. Endocr. Metab. Dis.*; 45 women, 50–65 yr, 3×/week for 12 weeks) found **HIIT** significantly cut **body weight (~3%)**, BMI, **body-fat % (~6%)**, and waist-to-hip ratio, and improved **triglycerides, total and LDL cholesterol, glucose, insulin, and HOMA-IR** vs. control. **Concurrent training (HIIT + resistance)** produced *greater* weight/BMI/fat-loss with similar metabolic gains — a strong case for pairing intervals with strength work.
- **Older women.** A 2026 RCT (*Women*, MDPI) of a supervised HIIT program (3 sessions/week) showed significant gains in **aerobic capacity**, **lower-limb strength (30-second chair-stand)**, and **mobility (Timed Up-and-Go)**, plus reductions in **body-fat % and visceral-fat index** and better quality of life — with **no major adverse events**.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and metabolic wins; **add strength training**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate. Supervised, individualized intensity (e.g., 90–95% max HR bouts) is how these trials got results.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's trials sharpen *how* to train and *when* to start.

- **Technique-specific training beats general movement.** A 2026 RCT in the *International Urogynecology Journal* compared PFMT with Pilates and Pilates + voluntary pelvic-floor contraction. **PFMT won across the board**: incontinence impact (ICIQ-SF) fell **−4.4 points** with PFMT vs. only **−0.7** with Pilates, and peak vaginal squeeze pressure rose **+24.4 mmHg** vs. ~6 mmHg. Directly training the muscle matters more than general core work.
- **Prevention works during pregnancy.** The multicenter **PEFLOW** RCT (*JAMA Network Open*; 764 first-time mothers) found a structured pelvic-floor workout **lowered postpartum SUI at 6 weeks (8.7% vs. 13.9%)** and nearly doubled the share of women reaching strong pelvic-floor strength.
- **For postpartum SUI, go combined.** A 2026 trial found **high-intensity combined PFMT** achieved the best strength grades and the **lowest 6-month recurrence** vs. focused or generalized training alone.
- **Add-on electrical stimulation.** A 2026 *Scientific Reports* RCT found adding **interferential current (IFC)** to supervised pelvic-floor exercises produced a specific extra reduction in **weekly incontinence episodes**, though most other measures improved similarly in both groups — a useful add-on, not a replacement.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sources.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training Outperforms Pilates in Women with Stress Urinary Incontinence: A Randomized Controlled Trial

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard treatment** — not a replacement for HER2-targeted therapy. Two themes stand out for HER2-positive, often **TP53/p53-altered**, disease.

- **A genetic vulnerability you can exploit.** A 2026 study (*npj Breast Cancer*) modeled **HER2;TP53 co-mutant** tumors and found they resist **neratinib** but stay **sensitive to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)** — specifically to its **TOP1-inhibitor payload (exatecan)**. Mechanistically, the p53 mutation drives **increased histone acetylation and open chromatin**, sensitizing cells to TOP1 inhibition via G2/M arrest and apoptosis. The **neratinib + T-DXd** combination was highly effective preclinically and is now in a **phase I trial (NCT05372614 / NCI ETCTN 10495)**. Translation: in this high-risk subtype, the payload chemistry — not just HER2 blockade — may be the key.
- **Supplements: mechanism vs. proof, and real interaction risk.** A 2026 systematic review on **nutritional supplements and antioxidants** flagged a **double-edged effect**: high-dose antioxidants may blunt the **reactive-oxygen-species pathways** some therapies rely on and, in parts of the data, correlated with **higher recurrence/mortality**. A second systematic review of **dietary supplements** found they were generally **not linked to serious harm** but offered mostly **quality-of-life/symptom** benefit rather than proven cancer-outcome gains. Coordinate any supplement (including antioxidants, vitamin D, omega-3s) with your oncology team **before** starting, especially during active treatment.

Important framing: the co-mutation finding is **preclinical**, and the supplement evidence is **mixed/observational**. Use integrative options as *clinician-approved add-ons*, never as substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or **disjointed/fragmented** sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements** — and, when medication is needed, favors the newer orexin-blocking class for fragmentation.

- **CBT-I is first-line; sleep hygiene alone is not enough.** A 2026 joint position statement from Australian sleep and primary-care bodies reaffirmed **multicomponent CBT-I** as first-line across settings, comorbidities, and delivery modes (including digital/self-guided). Medicines are **second-line or adjuncts**: benzodiazepines and **Z-drugs only ~2–4 weeks**, **melatonin** up to ~13 weeks, and **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** generally reserved for **chronic** insomnia. Sedating antihistamines, antipsychotics, and cannabinoids are **not recommended**.
- **Best class for fragmented sleep: orexin antagonists.** A phase-II PSG analysis showed **daridorexant** dose-dependently **reduced awakenings (NAW) and wake-after-sleep-onset**, cut light N1, and **increased N2, N3, and REM** — restoring architecture rather than just sedating. A 364-person RCT of **seltorexant** improved both **sleep initiation and maintenance** over 14 days, holding up better than **zolpidem** with **fewer adverse events**.
- **Supplements, honestly.** The **AASM** suggests **not** using **melatonin** for sleep-onset or maintenance insomnia (weak recommendation); it's most useful for **circadian** problems (jet lag, shift work) and as prolonged-release in adults ≥55. For **magnesium**, a 2026 systematic review (12 RCTs) found **inconsistent, low-certainty** evidence and does not support it as routine insomnia treatment; a 2025 RCT of **magnesium bisglycinate 250 mg** (n=155) showed only a **small** improvement in insomnia severity, mainly in people with **low dietary magnesium**.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to **rule out sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital) before chronic medication.
